title: README file
plain: A README is the first file a visitor reads. It says what the project does, how to run it and where to get help. It is usually named README.md in the top folder.
check: A friend opens your project folder for the first time. Which three questions must the README answer on its first screen?
rubric: States in one or two sentences what the project does
Gives the exact commands to install and run it, in order
Lists what must be installed first and where to ask for help
try: Open `README.md` in your project (create it in your editor if it is missing). Add three headings: `# Project name`, `## What it does` and `## How to run`. Under the last one, type the exact commands you use. Then follow your own steps in a fresh terminal window to check that they work.
pitfall: A README that only its author can follow is not finished: write down what must be installed and the exact commands, and test them from a fresh folder. On a public repository everyone can read it, so it never holds secrets.

title: Project folders and names
plain: A project layout is how files are grouped into folders, for example src for code, docs for notes and tests for checks. Clear, consistent names help you, other people and Codex find things.
check: A folder holds app.py, app_old.py, app_final.py and forty screenshots. What would you change in this folder, and why?
rubric: Groups files by purpose (code, tests, documentation, assets), with one kind of thing in each folder
Names files and folders in lowercase with hyphens or underscores, without spaces, and says what they contain
Names what stays out of the repository: secrets, downloaded libraries and build output
try: List the top level of your project with `ls` (macOS, Linux, Git Bash) or `dir` (PowerShell). Next to each entry write one word for its purpose: code, docs, tests, config or generated. Entries you cannot name are the first ones to ask Codex about. This step only reads; it changes nothing.
pitfall: Spaces, capital letters and accents in names cause errors in commands and links, and File.txt and file.txt are the same file on default Windows and macOS disks but two files on Linux. Use lowercase letters, digits, hyphens and underscores.

title: Small, frequent commits
plain: A small commit holds one logical change that works on its own. Frequent small commits give you save points to return to and make every change quick to read and to undo.
check: In one session you changed a button's colour, fixed a typo in the README and added a new page. How many commits would you make, and why?
rubric: Each commit has one purpose and the project still runs after it
Uses git add with file names, or git add -p, to put only that part in each commit
Writes a message for each commit that says what that commit does
try: Before your next change from Codex, run `git status` to make sure the last work is committed. After the change, run `git status` and `git diff --stat` (new files appear only in git status) and decide whether it has one purpose. If it does, commit it on its own with `git add <files>` and `git commit -m "..."`; if not, stage and commit the parts separately.
pitfall: People save up one big commit for when everything is finished, but until you commit Git cannot undo anything, and a huge commit hides which part broke the project. Commit whenever one small piece works.

title: Code review
plain: Code review means reading a change, from a person or Codex, before you accept it. Check what changed, whether it matches the request, and whether it adds risks such as secrets or deleted files.
check: Codex changed nine files for a request that sounded like a change to one file. What do you check before you accept it?
rubric: Starts with git status and git diff --stat to see which files changed or are new, and how large the change is
Checks each file against the request: scope, deleted files, new libraries, keys or secrets, and tests
Gives a decision with a reason and asks about anything not understood
try: After any change, run `git status` and `git diff --stat` for the list of files (new files appear only in git status). Then run `git diff <file>` for one file at a time and say aloud for each block what changed and why. If the output fills the screen, press `q` to leave the pager. Ask Codex about every block you cannot explain.
pitfall: A review is not only checking that the code runs: code can run and still delete files, add a risky library or contain a key. Read the diff for scope, secrets and surprises, whoever wrote it.

title: Versions and changelog
plain: Semantic versioning writes a version as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, for example 2.4.1: raise major for breaking changes, minor for new compatible features, patch for fixes. CHANGELOG.md lists the changes of each version.
check: Your project is at 1.4.2. You fix a typo bug, add an optional new setting and remove an old command, all in one release. What is the next version, and which change decided it?
rubric: Bug fix only: 1.4.3
New feature that keeps working with old use: 1.5.0 (patch goes back to 0)
Removed or changed behaviour that breaks users: 2.0.0
try: Create `CHANGELOG.md` with the heading `# Changelog`, a section `## [Unreleased]`, and under it the headings `### Added` and `### Fixed`. Write one real line for your latest change. At a release, rename `Unreleased` to the version and the date, for example `## [0.1.0] - 2026-10-07` (year-month-day).
pitfall: Versions 0.y.z are for early development, where anything may change. A changelog is also not a copy of git log: write for the people who use the project, newest version first, with groups such as Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security.

title: Project documentation
plain: Project documentation is written explanation kept with the code. It includes a README for newcomers, a docs folder for guides, comments for tricky lines, and short notes on why choices were made.
check: Where would you write down each of these: how to start the app, why you chose SQLite over another database, and what a strange pattern on line 40 does?
rubric: Install and run steps go in the README
The reason for a choice goes in a short decision note or docs page, and an odd line gets a comment that says why
Release history goes in the changelog, and a secret value goes nowhere in the repository
try: Open your project and look for `README.md`, a `docs` folder, and comments above tricky code. Write the one that is missing: three lines under `## How to run` in the README is a good start. Ask Codex for a draft if you like, then run every command in it yourself.
pitfall: Documentation that repeats what the code already says goes stale. Comments should explain why, not what, and docs that nobody runs go out of date: test the commands in your docs after each change.

title: Development and production
plain: An environment is a place where your program runs. Development is your own computer, where mistakes affect nobody else. Production is the live copy that real users use. Each needs separate data and keys.
check: Your app works on localhost but shows an error on the live site. Which three things can differ between the two places?
rubric: Names three differences between the two places: the data or database, the keys and settings (environment variables), and the versions or operating system
Reads the error message and the live site's logs before changing any code
Names one safeguard, such as separate .env files per environment, or not giving production keys to development tools
try: Open `.env.example` (or the README) of your project and list which settings would have different values on your computer and on a live site, for example the database address, the API keys and the web address. This step only reads; it changes nothing.
pitfall: Many beginners use one database and one set of keys for everything, so a mistake in development changes live data. Keep separate databases and keys, and never give production credentials to a development tool or an AI agent.

title: Deployment basics
plain: To deploy means to put a working copy of your project where other people can use it. It involves a build step, a host, secret settings on that host, and a check that it runs.
check: Before you put your project online, what would you prepare so that you can go back if the deploy goes wrong?
rubric: Confirms that the tests or a build pass locally and that all work is committed
Confirms that secrets are set on the host as settings, not stored in the code
Knows the live address and how to go back to the last working version
try: Write a short 'Deploy' section in your README and answer its five lines in your own words: Which command builds the project? Which command runs it? Which settings differ in production? Where do the secrets live there? How do I go back to the last working version?
pitfall: 'It works on my computer' is not a deployment test, because the host has a different operating system, other versions and other settings. Deploy from committed code with a repeatable command, and read the host's logs when it fails.

title: Hosting types
plain: Hosting means renting a computer that stays online. Static hosting serves ready-made files, an app platform runs your program for you, and a server (VPS) is a rented computer you manage yourself.
check: You have a recipe site made of HTML, CSS and images, and a second project with a login and a database. Which kind of hosting fits each?
rubric: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript pages: static hosting
A program with login and a database: an app platform, or a server with a database
Names one limit or cost to check before choosing, such as free-plan limits, sleeping apps or traffic caps
try: Answer three questions about your project in three lines: Does a program have to run all the time (yes or no)? Does it store data that users change (yes or no)? Is it only files that a browser can open (yes or no)? The three answers point to the hosting type.
pitfall: Free plans often have limits, such as apps that go to sleep, disks that are reset, traffic caps or rules about commercial use, and plans and prices change. On some platforms a file saved on the app's disk disappears at the next deploy; keep data in a database or a storage service.

title: Continuous integration
plain: Continuous integration (CI) runs your tests and checks automatically on a shared computer every time code is pushed. A failure shows up before the change reaches users.
check: A change shows a failed CI check, but the tests pass on your computer. What can explain that?
rubric: Finds the failed step in the run's log
Reads the first error message, not only the last line, and runs the same command on their own computer
Names one difference between the two places: tool versions, operating system, or a file or setting that exists only on their computer
try: If your repository is on GitHub, look for the folder `.github/workflows` in your project: `ls .github/workflows` (macOS, Linux, Git Bash) or `dir .github\workflows` (PowerShell). Each `.yml` or `.yaml` file is one automated workflow. Open one and find the `on:` line (when it runs) and the `run:` lines (what commands it runs). No folder means no CI yet.
pitfall: A green CI run only proves that the checks somebody wrote have passed, so with no tests it stays green for broken code. CI does not replace reading the change yourself.

title: Open-source license
plain: A license file tells other people what they may do with your code. Without one, copyright law keeps all rights with you, so a public repository without a license is not open source.
check: A friend says 'my repository is public, so anyone can reuse the code'. What does a missing LICENSE file mean for people who want to reuse it?
rubric: Says that without a license all rights stay with the author: others may view and fork a public repository on GitHub but may not reuse the code elsewhere
Decides first whether the project will be public and open (private code needs no license file)
Picks a standard license such as MIT or Apache-2.0 with choosealicense.com and saves the full text as LICENSE in the top folder
try: Open choosealicense.com in your browser, answer its questions for your project, and write two sentences each about MIT and Apache-2.0 in your own words. Do not add the file to a repository, or make a repository public, until you have decided. A license choice is a legal choice and this is not legal advice.
pitfall: A public repository without a license can be viewed and forked on GitHub, but other people have no permission to reuse the code elsewhere; private code needs no license. A license covers only your own code, because libraries you use keep their own licenses.

title: Issue tracking
plain: An issue is a written, numbered note about one bug, idea or task. A good bug issue has a clear title, exact steps to reproduce it, what you expected and what happened.
check: How would you rewrite the issue title 'login broken' so that the person who fixes it can start work?
rubric: The title names the problem in one line
The steps to reproduce are numbered and exact
It states the expected result, the actual result, and where it happened (version, operating system)
try: Draft one issue for a real problem in your project in a text file `issue-draft.md`: a title, numbered steps, what you expected, and what happened. Then ask yourself whether a stranger could reproduce the problem from your text alone.
pitfall: Issues are not only complaints: they also hold ideas and tasks, one topic per issue, and they do not close by themselves. On GitHub, writing Fixes #12 in a pull request description closes issue 12, but only when that pull request is merged into the default branch.

title: Backups: data and code
plain: A backup is a separate copy you can restore from. Git and GitHub protect committed code, but not ignored files such as .env, local databases, uploads or data folders.
check: Your laptop is stolen tonight. Which parts of your project could you get back from GitHub, and which would be gone?
rubric: Names the code (committed and pushed) as protected
Names ignored or generated files (a database file, uploads, .env, API keys) as not protected by Git
Describes where the data is copied to and plans one test restore
try: Run `git status --ignored` in your project and read the `Ignored files` list. Everything on that list exists only on this computer. Next to each entry write: can I recreate it? If not, it needs a backup somewhere else.
pitfall: Learners think GitHub is a backup of everything, but it holds only what was committed and pushed; ignored files, local databases and keys are not there. A backup that was never restored is only a hope, so restore one test copy once.
